extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent applicants, patent agents, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and examining the specification/description of a patent application under the Canadian Patent Act and Patent Rules, focusing on content, form, enablement and support for claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must provide a clear and complete disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must provide a clear and complete disclosure of the invention such that the person skilled in the art: can unambiguously identify what has been invented; and is enabled to practice this invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes and authority emphasize disclosure as the quid pro quo for patent exclusivity. The description must answer “What is your invention?: How does it work?” and must allow the public (person skilled in the art) to make the same successful use of the invention as the inventor could at filing/publication. See Consolboard and Supreme Court authority cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper disclosure — statutory requirements (subsection 27(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification of an invention must: correctly and fully describe the invention and its operation or use as contemplated by the inventor; set out clearly the various steps in a process, or the method of constructing, making, compounding or using a machine, manufacture or composition of matter, in such full, clear, concise and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it pertains, or with which it is most closely connected, to make, construct, compound or use it; in the case of a machine, explain the principle of the machine and the best mode in which the inventor has contemplated the application of that principle; and in the case of a process, explain the necessary sequence, if any, of the various steps, so as to distinguish the invention from other inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory bullets are treated as the baseline legal requirements for a description. Examiners and drafters must ensure each element is addressed. The requirement to enable must be judged relative to a person skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must be correct, full, clear and accurate (no misleading statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be correct; that means both clear and accurate. It must be free from avoidable obscurity or ambiguity and must be as simple and distinct as the difficulty of description permits. It must not contain erroneous or misleading statements calculated to deceive or mislead the persons to whom the specification is addressed and render it difficult for them without trial and experiment to comprehend in what manner the invention is to be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description must give all information necessary for successful operation without leaving result to chance. Warnings must be given where required. Inventor must act uberrima fide and disclose information known to enable the invention to be carried out to its best effect. See Minerals Separation summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressee: person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is directed to a person skilled in the art (a fictional construct) who is competent, an average logical but unimaginative worker, reasonably diligent in keeping up with advances, and who interprets the disclosure with a mind willing to understand and desirous of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging sufficiency, identify the appropriate skilled person (may be a team). Examiners must attempt to interpret application and prior art using the knowledge that skilled person would have at the relevant date. The skilled person may be presumed expert-level in a highly technical field but is not creative or intuitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description may be supplemented by common general knowledge (but must be complete as of filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A description sufficient to allow the person skilled in the art to practice the invention is enabling; it need not teach what is plainly obvious to the skilled person. The skilled person's common general knowledge is brought to bear as of the date the application came into their possession (the publication date), but the invention must still be fully described as of the filing date and utility established no later than that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although common general knowledge at publication may expand what is enabling, one cannot rely on post-filing developments to cure a disclosure that was insufficient as filed. Inventive possession and utility must be established by filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading or erroneous explicit instructions defeat sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: If a description includes statements that direct the person skilled in the art to attempt to practice the invention in a manner contrary to their common general knowledge, the skilled person will follow them; where such disclosed manner will not work to achieve the promise of the invention, the description does not comply with subsection 27(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilled person will overlook obvious errors or omissions that can be readily corrected, but explicit misleading directions that lead to failure render the disclosure insufficient. See cross-reference to guidance on misleading definitions (14.05.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled must not be required to solve problems requiring undue burden or inventive ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilled person can be called upon to perform routine experiments, but must be able to practice the full scope of the invention without undue burden or the need to exercise inventive ingenuity; if undue burden or inventive step is required the description is insufficient and claims unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine testing to verify predictable characteristics is permitted; discovering unexpected, unpredictable properties is not routine. Examples: (1) defining a flange by ductility range is acceptable if skilled person can test or know suitable metals; (2) claiming a drug by a desirable release profile without guidance to other compounds that achieve it may be insufficient because identifying others may require inventive effort. The inquiry focuses on whether identifying suitable embodiments requires invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of the invention not generally required (except where sound prediction depends on it)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally not necessary for the description to provide a theory as to why the invention operates as it does; the requirement is that the description teaches what the invention is and how to make it operate to provide the promised benefits. However, where utility is predicated on sound prediction and the line of reasoning depends on the theory, that theory may need to be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical readers want to know that it works and how to work it. If the applicant relies on a predictive argument for utility, disclose the reasoning/theory underlying the prediction so the skilled person can assess it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose the solution to a practical problem (technical problem and solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must put the person skilled in the art in a position to appreciate the nature of the problem being solved and the solution provided. A description must be set out in terms that permit the technical problem and its solution to be understood, even if the problem is not expressly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solution must be in a practical form (elements that interact with the physical world) and include all elements necessary to provide the utility. Novel elements and novel combinations must be fully described, and the description must teach their interrelationship so the 'wheels will go round' without requiring modification by the skilled person. External documents may be referred to, but the invention must be described and enabled by the description alone in view of common general knowledge. Inventive ingenuity cannot post-date filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations must yield a unitary result (not a mere aggregation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is an assemblage of parts whose conjoint use leads to a result different from the sum of the results of the elements (a unitary result). A mere placing side-by-side of old integers where each performs its own function independently is not a patentable combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unitary result (utility) of the combination must be established by demonstration or sound prediction. If structure is described but the unitary result is not clear, the description may need to explicitly describe the result to distinguish it from a mere aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional limitations must be scrutinized for support and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language (in claims or description) is not per se objectionable but is used to provide breadth and must be considered from the perspective of the skilled person: can the skilled person practice the full breadth without undue experimentation or inventive ingenuity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If means to effect the function are common general knowledge, functional limitation is less likely to be objectionable. If few or only one means is known, broad functional language may improperly claim speculative embodiments. Examples: a broad 'hair-growth activating compound' claim when only one compound is known is objectionable; defining a second component as 'NSAID' when that class and its members are well understood is acceptable; 'cutting means' can be acceptable if appropriate cutting means are known to skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirements for biotechnological inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain biotech inventions may require a sequence listing of nucleotide or amino acid sequences to be included with the description or a deposit of biological material with an International Depository Authority for the description to be considered sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See detailed requirements in subsections 23.05.07 and 23.06 for sequence listings and deposits. Failure to comply with these specific disclosure obligations can render biotech descriptions insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant as their own lexicographer — definitions in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant can act as their own lexicographer: if they plainly tell the reader that for the purpose of the specification a particular word is used with a specified meaning, that definition will be applied. However, such drafting is awkward and undesirable unless intention is made plain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During examination terms are given their plain and usual meaning unless the description clearly defines them otherwise. Definitions contrary to the usual meaning in the art that cause confusion or ambiguity are objectionable. Narrowing definitions for expediency that do not sacrifice clarity (e.g. defining 'ethylene polymer' with exact compositional limits) are generally acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure by reference to trademarked products
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming a trademarked product is not equivalent to describing the composition of that product. Knowing components of a trademarked product does not necessarily identify which component is essential to the invention's role. If an invention is described only in terms of a trademarked product, proper support must be carefully considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If composition of the trademarked product is not known and the product is not commercially available, the invention is not enabled. Examples that rely on trademarked products of undisclosed composition do not automatically embody the invention; the applicant must have been aware of the composition no later than the filing date. Composition not in the prior art as of filing cannot be added later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must not state the invention by reference to the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper for the description to state the nature of the invention by reference to the claims (e.g., 'the problem is overcome through the method of claim 1'). The description must correctly and fully describe the invention in the body of the specification itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cross-referential statements suggest the description does not correctly and fully disclose the invention and are objectionable under subsection 27(3). Amending the description to include language of originally filed claims in a non-divisional application can be compliant under subsection 38.2(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: References to foreign practice or law should be avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements whose correctness depends on foreign patent prosecution practices or laws may be inaccurate or misleading in the context of Canadian law and should be removed; e.g., indicating an application is a continuation-in-part or divisional of a foreign patent document is incorrect in Canadian context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements may be viewed as incorrect and therefore a defect under subsection 27(3). Statements regarding rights of foreign governments or foreign procedure must be checked and removed if inaccurate. See cross-reference to 14.09 and 14.08 for related issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of the description (section 56 of the Patent Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must include the following information, in the following manner and order: (a) a short, precise title (no trademark/coin/personal name); (b) the technical field; (c) background art important for understanding/searching/examination; (d) a description permitting the technical problem and its solution to be understood; (e) concise description of figures (if any); (f) at least one mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention, using examples and references to drawings if appropriate; and (g) a sequence listing, if required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection 56(2) allows different order/presentation if, given the invention's nature, it results in better understanding or more economical presentation (e.g., prior-art drawings described with background). Title should be descriptive (e.g., 'flame-retardant rigid polyurethane foam' rather than 'foam'). Office uses description title as correct title; divergence in database is not a defect but may be noted by examiner.
